Screeps: World, developed and published by Screeps, LLC, is a strategy game that fundamentally redefines what it means to “play” an RTS. Rather than directly commanding units in real time, players are tasked with writing JavaScript code that governs every action their colony performs. This single design decision transforms the experience into something far more cerebral than traditional strategy titles, where success depends not on reflexes or multitasking speed, but on logic, planning, and the ability to build efficient, self-sustaining systems.

At its core, the game places players in a persistent online world where they must establish and expand a colony across a grid of interconnected rooms. Resources are gathered, structures are built, and defenses are maintained, but all of these processes are handled by autonomous units known as creeps. Instead of issuing commands manually, players write scripts that define how these units behave—how they harvest energy, transport resources, construct buildings, and engage enemies. Once deployed, this code continues to run even when the player is offline, meaning the colony evolves continuously based on the quality of its underlying logic.

This approach creates a unique form of strategy where the primary challenge lies in designing systems rather than executing actions. Early on, players may write simple scripts to handle basic tasks, but as the game progresses, the complexity increases significantly. Managing larger territories requires more advanced code capable of handling logistics, prioritizing tasks, and responding to dynamic threats. Over time, players often refine their scripts into highly optimized systems, turning their colonies into efficient, automated networks. This iterative process—writing, testing, debugging, and improving—becomes the central loop of the game, offering a level of depth that few strategy titles can match.

The persistent, massively multiplayer environment adds another layer of complexity. Thousands of players share the same world, competing for space and resources while forming alliances or engaging in conflicts. Because everything operates in real time, the state of the world is constantly changing, and players must adapt their systems to survive in an environment shaped by both AI and human opponents. This creates a sense of ongoing progression that feels meaningful, as every improvement to your code directly impacts your colony’s ability to thrive over the long term.

However, this depth comes with a significant barrier to entry. Screeps: World assumes a willingness to engage with programming at a fairly fundamental level, and while basic JavaScript knowledge is enough to get started, the game quickly demands more advanced problem-solving skills. Even with tutorials and documentation available, the learning curve can be steep, particularly for players without prior coding experience. It is a game that requires patience and persistence, and it does little to simplify its systems for newcomers.

In terms of presentation, the game is functional rather than visually impressive. The interface is designed to support coding and system management, providing the tools necessary to monitor and adjust your colony, but it lacks the cinematic flair or polish of more traditional RTS games. For many players, this will be a minor concern, as the real appeal lies in the underlying systems and the satisfaction of seeing well-written code perform as intended. Watching a complex network of behaviors operate smoothly can be just as rewarding as any visual spectacle.

One of the most compelling aspects of Screeps: World is how it blurs the line between game and practical skill-building. Players often find themselves improving their programming abilities as they play, learning to think more efficiently and structure their code more effectively. This gives the experience a unique dual purpose: it is both a game and a creative, problem-solving exercise. However, this also means that enjoyment is closely tied to an interest in coding; those who do not find satisfaction in writing and refining scripts may struggle to stay engaged.

Ultimately, Screeps: World is a deeply specialized experience that rewards a particular kind of player. It is not designed for casual enjoyment or immediate gratification, but for those who appreciate systems, optimization, and the process of building something that can operate independently. Its complexity and steep learning curve may limit its appeal, but for players willing to invest the time, it offers a uniquely engaging and intellectually rewarding take on the strategy genre.

I've enjoyed playing this game quite a bit. It can feel daunting at first if you haven't programmed before but it's helped me a lot. I would recommend reading through the API and documentation because it provides a lot of useful starter code for your bot.

The screeps community discord is very active where you can chat, ask for help, or get updates on conflicts around the map.

It's an RTS game where you claim areas on the map and you gather resources, trade with others, fight or form alliances, or just keep to yourself and develop at your own pace.

The catch though is that you have to write code for every unit, structure, or resource in the game so that they can function and interact with each other and everything persists while you're offline. Your rooms can get destroyed but the main enjoyment is watching your code base grow and prosper into a more advanced empire over time. Every new update you create for your empire is exciting

Since the game requires you to write code, it takes time to have a decent empire but if you're someone who wants to sit down and solve challenges and become a better programmer or just learn to code, this game is fantastic.

The main screeps world version of the game is all you need to play. You can join shard 3 (kind of known as the beginner shard) where you won't be at any disadvantage because the CPU is maxed at 20. If you decide to venture past shard 3, you will probably want the lifetime CPU unlock so you don't reach your CPU limit which causes your units to not act during that tick until your CPU regenerates back. Although some players have 30+ rooms with just 20 CPU, I can only manage about 5 before running into issues but you won't have to worry about that problem anyways when you first start out.

Screeps Arena is separate from the MMO. Think of it as quick matchmaking where your bot competes against another player.

And then seasons are where players spawn in and compete against each other based on the season's objectives. Each one lasts about 2 months and may have about 40-50 players depending on how many people decide to participate. You can buy season tickets with in-game currency or you can buy them with real money.

Your bot can also technically make you real money by generating pixels (an in-game currency) and using them to create decorations and then selling those decorations on steam. Each decoration may be a couple cents to a couple dollars depending on how rare it is.

Overall it's a really cool and unique game It's a perfect game to play and come back to after a few months on and off. If your economy is really strong, you can get a room to max level in a few days.

Screeps – A game that rewards thinking, not grinding

Screeps is not a traditional game, and that is exactly its strength.

There is no story to follow, no levels to rush through, and no “win screen” waiting at the end. Instead, Screeps offers a persistent world where your code is the player, and your job is to design systems that survive, adapt, and improve over time.

What makes Screeps special is that it doesn’t test your reflexes or your ability to memorize mechanics. It tests your ability to think in systems:

How do you keep something running when parts fail?

How do you prioritize under limited resources?

How do you avoid complexity turning into chaos?

The game is brutally honest.
If your logic is fragile, your colony collapses.
If your assumptions are wrong, time will expose them.

This makes Screeps deeply educational, but not in a “tutorial” way. You don’t learn programming because the game explains it to you. You learn because the world reacts to your decisions continuously, even when you are offline.

It’s also worth noting what Screeps is not:

It’s not casual.

It’s not fast gratification.

It’s not about constant competition unless you choose it to be.

If you enjoy reflection, long-term thinking, automation, and building something that can run calmly without constant intervention, Screeps is incredibly rewarding. If you want instant action or hand-holding, it probably isn’t.

Screeps feels less like a game you “play” and more like a laboratory for autonomy, resilience, and system design. That’s rare. And that’s why it deserves to be played.

It's an incredibly fun and challenging game if you're a programmer looking to do something fun with programming.

In my opinion, it's even good preparation to learn video game programming.

Many of the mindsets you have to learn to "play" Screeps well will also serve you well while programming your own video game.
[list]
    [*]Your code runs in a main loop that starts from the beginning every frame.
    [*]Therefore you cannot animate or progress your entities in loops like you would in a web page. Your inner loops hold up the current tick just like they would hold up the current frame in a video game.
    [*]Therefore you have to read the state of everything once per frame, track your goals, increment progress towards completing them, and then save it and start over again.
    [*]One of the resources you must manage is CPU usage. Therefore, also like a video game, you have to write efficient code. For example, you shouldn't generate a path for your entities to follow every turn. You generate it once, save it to memory, and then make them step along it frame-by-frame.
[/list]
See what I mean?

This game could be a lifelong hobby if you can get past the steep learning curve.

Some people download someone else's code and modify it, but I recommend writing it yourself from scratch.

It's far more rewarding when you see your units moving around and doing stuff, and you know it was your blood, sweat, and tears that made it happen.
